item.title: Predicting Realized Variance Out of Sample: Can Anything Beat The Benchmark?
item.description: arXiv:2506.07928v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The discrepancy between realized volatility and the market's view of volatility has been known to predict individual equity options at the monthly horizon. It is not clear how this predictability depends on a forecast's ability to predict firm-level volatility. We consider this phenomenon at the daily frequency using high-dimensional machine learning models, as well as low-dimensional factor models. We find that marginal improvements to standard forecast error measurements can lead to economically significant gains in portfolio performance. This makes a case for re-imagining the way we train models that are used to construct portfolios.
item.dc:creator: Austin Pollok

item.title: Volatility Forecasts with Market Trends
item.description: arXiv:2606.20145v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show how volatility forecasts for financial markets can be refined by accounting for the current trends in these markets. Empirically, volatilities tend to increase day after day in times of strong up- or down-trends. This effect is particularly pronounced during down-trends. We find that it can accurately be modeled by including quadratic polynomials of the current trend strength as explanatory factors. Such factors can improve the predictive power of a wide range of volatility models, ranging from linear EWMA-based models over GARCH models and range-based models to stochastic volatility models. Our results are based on a robust statistical analysis of three decades of daily futures prices across equity-, bond-, FX- and commodity markets.
item.dc:creator: Sara A. Safari, Christoph Schmidhuber

item.title: Evaluating LLM Research Agents as Tests of Return Predictability
item.description: arXiv:2611.04070v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How often do research agents built on large language models report that they can forecast returns when the data contain no signal? We score the conclusions of four such agents as statistical decisions on the same simulated monthly return series. Without a prescribed significance level, the agents reported that their forecasts would beat the expanding historical mean in 16-44% of 110 null samples, whereas a Holm-adjusted regression test rejected the absence of predictability in 8% of the same samples. When a weak predictor was present, comparisons at matched false-positive rates did not establish a detection advantage for the three commercial agents. Instructing those agents to report outperformance only if they would reject the absence of predictability at the 5% level, accounting for every specification they evaluated, reduced their false-positive rates to 0-3%. It also reduced detection at a population $R^2$ of 1%: from 74% to 45% for Claude Opus 5.5, from 59% to 6% for GPT-6.1 Sol and from 71% to 15% for GPT-6.1 Terra. Whether the instruction holds the false-positive rate at 5% remains unresolved. For researchers who delegate the search for return predictors to an agent, specifying the final comparison deserves as much attention as choosing the forecasting model.
item.dc:creator: Chang Liu
